o1.biggest_strength: A clean, plain-language split of proved facts from checks, with working that traces to my data: Meta would have blended to about $79, a loss of $33 per first order, and $94 as the 18-month breakeven. Every check and move has an owner.
o1.biggest_mistake: Moves are ranked by High/Medium/Low rather than a single gross-profit number, and the '$100k cut adds $23k to $41k' line is loosely supported. I can't tell how much each move is worth to the board's contribution goal.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Size each move in contribution points or dollars with the working shown, add action thresholds to the scorecard, and give a firm contribution target instead of 'set a baseline in week 1'.

o2.biggest_strength: It rebuilds a contribution baseline (7.8% now against 13.6% a year ago) and sizes every move in contribution points with low, likely and high cases. That is the exact lens the board asked for.
o2.biggest_mistake: It is dense and a little jargon-heavy (gain ranges, week 4/8 lines, stacked assumptions). The 'practitioner yardstick' on flows and the dated calendar are not grounded in my data.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Keep the quantified ranking but write it in plainer words with fewer stacked assumptions, and drop the ungrounded benchmark.

reason: Both find the same causes: Meta cost, the linen shrink and the half-off email. Output 2 turns them into a contribution-margin baseline, sizes each move with working, and adds a post-purchase survey and a swatch-kit test. It keeps the brand safe by not using the 'nice hotel' line in ads or running sitewide discounts, and it gives action thresholds on the scorecard. Output 1 is easier to read, but its ranking is vaguer.
